title: How a Plane Overhead Can Reveal Where You Filmed
h1: How a plane overhead can give away where a video was filmed
question: Can the sound of a plane overhead reveal where a video was filmed?
answer: Sometimes, yes. In November 2026 a YouTuber, Colsto, showed that the faint hum of passing propeller planes in a video's audio can be matched against public flight-tracking data. Each plane's pitch falls as it passes, and the shape of that fall depends on where you were standing. The name for this is the Doppler effect.

artefact.text: Colsto's own video walks through the method on a real recording and narrows it to one location. Gizmodo's report covers it in detail.

timeline.text: Gizmodo reports Colsto's method: match the Doppler curves of passing aircraft in a recording to ADS-B flight data.
Bruce Schneier picks it up on Schneier on Security.

mechanism.h: A plane hums at a steady pitch
mechanism.text: A propeller aircraft gives off a tone that, from the cockpit, doesn't change.

mechanism.h: On the ground, the pitch slides
mechanism.text: As the plane approaches, each sound wave leaves from a little closer to you than the last, so the waves bunch up and the pitch is higher. As it flies away they stretch out and the pitch drops. That is the Doppler effect.
The drop isn't instant. It is an S-shaped curve centred on the moment the plane is closest to you, and its shape depends on how fast the plane is going and how close it passes.
Aircraft with ADS-B broadcast their position, and public archives keep those tracks, so for any moment you can know which planes were in the sky and where.

For each candidate spot, predict the curve every logged plane would have made there, and keep the spots where the predictions match the recording. In Gizmodo's account, about 70,000 candidate locations fell to about 15,000 on timing and coverage checks, then curve-fitting picked a single location.

calc.assumptions: Illustrative numbers, not Colsto's: a 100 Hz engine tone, a plane at 60 m/s, sound at 343 m/s, still air, and the sound's travel time ignored.
points: The pitch falls from 121.2 Hz on approach to 85.1 Hz going away, a drop of 36.1 Hz. That total drop depends only on the plane's speed, not on where you stand.

Where you stand sets how steep the drop is. At 300 m from the flight path it falls at 3.5 Hz per second at its steepest; at 1 km, 1.05 Hz per second. The same plane takes about 3.3 times as long to make the drop.
So the size of the drop gives the speed, and the steepness gives the distance. Two planes on known tracks, each giving a distance, narrow you down to a few points on the map.
calc.formula: f(t) = f0 · c / (c + v·x / √(x² + d²)), with x = v·t; steepest slope = f0·v² / (c·d)

predict.q: The same plane, at the same speed, passes you twice: once 300 m away and once 1 km away. Which recording has the steeper drop in pitch?
predict.reveal: The 300 m pass, by about 3.3 times. The total drop is identical; only its steepness changes. That difference is what lets the recording place you.

predictions.text: Video-privacy advice will start treating background audio like metadata: something to strip before posting, alongside faces and GPS tags.

limits: It needs aircraft loud enough to pick out of the audio, and flight logs for that place and time.
Gizmodo notes it needs a way to narrow the flight data first; sound alone is a needle in a haystack.
Removing the audio track removes the curves this method reads.

faqs.q: Can a plane's sound reveal where a video was filmed?
faqs.a: In some cases. The pitch of each passing plane falls in a curve whose shape depends on where you stood. Matching those curves to public flight-tracking data can narrow a recording to a location, as Colsto demonstrated in November 2026.
A plot of how a moving source's pitch changes over time as heard by someone standing still. For a passing plane it is an S-shaped fall, centred on the moment of closest approach.
A system in which equipped aircraft broadcast their own position. Public archives record those broadcasts, which is what lets a recording's aircraft be matched to real flights.

faqs.q: Would muting the video stop this?
faqs.a: Removing the audio track removes the curves this method reads. Visual clues are a separate matter.
